prompt: A money-transfer service calls a Lua script via `EVAL` on EVERY request — throughput is 2000 transactions/second, and the team notices unusually high bandwidth to Redis. Optimize the code below, and explain the new operational risk introduced after the optimization and how to handle it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The problem is `EVAL` sending the ENTIRE script body over the network on every call; at 2000 req/s, the same few-hundred-byte script is sent millions of times per hour, wasting bandwidth on the hot path. The optimization: at startup, call `SCRIPT LOAD` ONCE so Redis compiles and caches the script, returning a SHA1 (40 hex characters); from then on every request calls `EVALSHA sha 2 src dst amount` — sending only 40 bytes instead of the whole script body, and Redis looks it up in its internal script cache to run it. The new risk: if Redis restarts or someone runs `SCRIPT FLUSH`, the script cache is wiped — the SHA the client holds still "looks valid" but Redis no longer recognizes it, so `EVALSHA` returns a `NOSCRIPT` error. Handle it by catching that error and falling back: retry with `EVAL` for that one request (or re-`SCRIPT LOAD` then retry `EVALSHA`), ensuring the request doesn't hard-fail when the cache is lost — many Redis clients (including some ioredis setups) automate this fallback step. Measure the gain by comparing average bandwidth/latency at the same throughput before/after, and separately test the `NOSCRIPT` scenario by simulating a Redis cache flush between calls.
